# Figure catalog — jitter sensitivity sweep

## figJ1 — Jitter sensitivity

**File:** `figures/main/figJ1_jitter_sensitivity.png`
**Source:** `results/jitter_sensitivity.csv`; panel C additionally reads
`results/glmcc/sensitivity/adj_{animal}_baseline.csv` and recomputes per-cell spike counts from
the gapped trains.
**Generated by:** `scripts/plot_jitter_sensitivity.py`

### Why this figure exists

The ±25 ms jitter control produced a single number (100.0% survival) that could be read either as
"the edges are not synaptic" or "25 ms was the wrong displacement". A single point cannot
distinguish those. This figure shows the whole curve, bounded below by a condition in which no
timing structure survives at all, so the reading is no longer ambiguous.

### Panels

**A — Edge survival vs displacement.** Grey lines are the 13 animals; blue is mean ± SD. The red
dashed curve is a **schematic** of what a synaptic edge set would have to look like — it is drawn
for scale and is not fitted or measured. The inset replots the measured curve on its own axis
(95–100%), because at the scale needed to show the synaptic expectation the real curve is a flat
line at the top of the plot. `full shuffle` is set apart from the millisecond axis by a dotted
rule: it is a category, not a displacement.

*What to notice:* the blue curve does not descend. Not at 5 ms, not at 100 ms, and not when every
spike is redrawn at random inside its window.

**B — Weight agreement vs displacement.** Pearson r between baseline and jittered weights over
surviving edges. Same layout.

*What to notice:* r stays above 0.999 through 100 ms and is still 0.96 ± 0.05 after a full
shuffle. The conclusion does not depend on the edge-presence threshold — the underlying weights
are nearly unchanged too.

**C — What the edge set does depend on.** Distribution of $\log_{10}(n_i n_j)$ for pairs that do
and do not receive an edge, three animals. Boxes are median and IQR, whiskers 1.5 × IQR, outliers
suppressed.

*What to notice:* the blue (edge) boxes sit above the grey (no edge) boxes with little overlap.
In day3 the medians differ by a factor of 693.

### Caption requirements

A caption must state: (i) n = 13 animals, aligned-ongoing arm, one jitter draw per level at seed
42; (ii) that survival is measured against the unjittered run of the same arm and that the 0 ms
level reproduces it exactly; (iii) that the red curve in A is schematic; (iv) that panel C is
three animals, not thirteen; (v) that `full shuffle` preserves per-cell per-window spike counts
and destroys all finer structure.

### Interpretation checklist

- [x] 0 ms reproduces the baseline exactly — machinery validated
- [x] a floor condition is present (full shuffle), so flatness is interpretable
- [x] error bars defined (SD across animals)
- [x] the schematic curve is labelled as such in the figure legend and here
- [x] spike retention reported separately so edge loss cannot be confused with spike loss
- [x] panel C gives the alternative explanation rather than leaving a bare negative

### What it changes

The figure moves the claim from "the 25 ms control failed" to "the edge set carries no
spike-timing information at any scale". That is a stronger and more actionable statement: it
rules out the synaptic interpretation for these matrices rather than casting doubt on one
control, and panel C names the variable that actually drives edge presence.

### Caveats

- Schematic red curve (see above) — the most likely thing to be misread.
- Panel A's main axis is dominated by the schematic; the inset carries the measurement. Anyone
  reading only the main axis will conclude "flat" correctly but will not see the 0.4-point shuffle
  effect.
- Panel C mixes animals with very different unit counts and firing rates; absolute
  $n_i n_j$ values are not comparable across the three, only the within-animal separation is.
- One arm (aligned-ongoing) only.
